interactions.label: Which clinical feature is the defining characteristic that distinguishes cluster

params.question: Which clinical feature is the defining characteristic that distinguishes cluster headache from migraine and tension-type headache?

answers.text: Bilateral, pressing pain of mild to moderate intensity

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Bilateral pressing pain is the hallmark of tension-type headache, not cluster headache.

answers.text: Unilateral pulsating pain worsened by routine physical activity

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Unilateral pulsating pain aggravated by activity is characteristic of migraine, not cluster headache.

answers.text: Ipsilateral autonomic features such as lacrimation and nasal congestion

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Ipsilateral autonomic activation — tearing, nasal congestion, and partial Horner syndrome — is the defining feature that sets cluster headache apart from other primary headache syndromes.

answers.text: Nausea and sensitivity to both light and sound during attacks

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Nausea with photophobia and phonophobia is characteristic of migraine attacks.

overallFeedback.feedback: The key separator is ipsilateral autonomic activation — tearing, nasal congestion, and partial Horner syndrome. This places cluster headache among the trigeminal autonomic cephalalgias.
Well done. Cluster headache belongs to the trigeminal autonomic cephalalgias because ipsilateral parasympathetic activation produces its distinctive autonomic signs.

interactions.label: A normal non-contrast CT brain scan is sufficient to exclude subarachnoid haemor

params.question: A normal non-contrast CT brain scan is sufficient to exclude subarachnoid haemorrhage in a patient presenting with thunderclap headache.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: A normal CT alone is not sufficient. The complete protocol requires a lumbar puncture at least 12 hours after onset when CT is negative. Both must be normal to exclude subarachnoid haemorrhage, given the life-threatening re-bleed risk.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct. A normal CT must be followed by a lumbar puncture performed at least 12 hours after onset. Only when both are normal can subarachnoid haemorrhage be excluded. Re-bleed risk within 24 hours is 20–30%, with missed re-bleed mortality of 40–50%.

params.question: A patient reports worsening headaches that are worst upon waking. Fundoscopy reveals papilloedema. Based on the Monro-Kellie doctrine, what best explains the morning pattern?

answers.text: Overnight dehydration concentrates pain mediators in the cerebrospinal fluid

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Dehydration does not explain morning headache in raised intracranial pressure. The mechanism relates to venous dynamics in the supine position.

answers.text: Increased venous return from the supine position overnight raises intracranial pressure

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The skull is a closed box with fixed total volume. Lying flat increases venous return to the cranium, raising intracranial pressure and worsening headache overnight.

answers.text: Cortisol levels are lowest in the early morning, reducing the pain threshold

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Cortisol is actually highest in the early morning. The morning headache of raised ICP is explained by increased venous return in the supine position, not hormonal variation.

answers.text: Melatonin released during sleep sensitises the trigeminal nerve endings

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: There is no established trigeminal sensitisation by melatonin. Morning headache in raised ICP results from supine positioning increasing venous return within the closed cranial cavity.

overallFeedback.feedback: The Monro-Kellie doctrine states that brain, CSF, and blood occupy a fixed total volume within the rigid skull. Lying flat overnight increases venous return, raising intracranial pressure and producing the characteristic morning headache.

Excellent. The Monro-Kellie doctrine — brain, CSF, and blood share a fixed volume in the rigid skull — explains why the supine position worsens pressure, making morning the worst time for these headaches.

interactions.label: Two patients both show lymphocytic pleocytosis and elevated protein in their CSF

params.question: Two patients both show lymphocytic pleocytosis and elevated protein in their CSF. Patient A has normal CSF glucose; Patient B has a markedly low CSF-to-serum glucose ratio. Which parameter is the key separator between these two patterns?

answers.text: Cell type — viral meningitis produces neutrophils, not lymphocytes

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Both viral and tuberculous meningitis typically show lymphocytic predominance in the CSF. Cell type alone does not distinguish them.

answers.text: Protein level — it is always normal in viral meningitis

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Protein can be mildly elevated in viral meningitis as well. While TB meningitis tends to produce higher protein, this is not the definitive separator.

answers.text: CSF glucose — normal in viral meningitis, low in tuberculous meningitis

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Normal CSF glucose is the key separator for viral meningitis. When glucose falls in the setting of lymphocytic pleocytosis, tuberculous meningitis must be strongly considered.

answers.text: Opening pressure — it is always elevated in tuberculous meningitis

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Opening pressure may be elevated in tuberculous meningitis, but it can also rise in other conditions such as cryptococcal meningitis. CSF glucose is the defining difference.

overallFeedback.feedback: The crucial differentiator is CSF glucose. Viral meningitis characteristically preserves normal glucose, while tuberculous meningitis drives it down — this single parameter often tips the diagnostic balance.
Well done. In clinical practice, a lymphocytic CSF with normal glucose strongly favours a viral aetiology, while a drop in glucose shifts the differential toward tuberculous or fungal causes.

interactions.label: A 30-year-old woman has migraine on 6 days per month with significant disability

params.question: A 30-year-old woman has migraine on 6 days per month with significant disability. She has been taking ibuprofen on 18 days per month for 4 months. What is the most appropriate initial step?

answers.text: Start propranolol 80 mg daily alongside the current analgesic regimen

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Adding preventive therapy without first addressing medication overuse is ineffective. The overuse cycle must be broken before prophylaxis can work.

answers.text: Withdraw the overused analgesic before initiating preventive therapy

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Preventive therapy must begin only after medication-overuse headache detoxification. Analgesic overuse (≥15 days/month for ≥3 months) paradoxically worsens headaches.

answers.text: Switch ibuprofen to sumatriptan for more effective acute relief

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Switching to another acute medication does not solve the overuse problem. Triptans carry the same risk of medication-overuse headache at 10 or more days per month.

answers.text: Prescribe topiramate 100 mg daily and continue the current analgesic

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Adding topiramate without first withdrawing the overused analgesic will not break the medication-overuse headache cycle. Detoxification must come first.

overallFeedback.feedback: The critical step is detoxification from the overused analgesic first. Painkillers taken on more than 10–15 days per month cause more headaches, not fewer. Preventive therapy succeeds only after the overuse cycle is broken.
Excellent. Medication-overuse headache is the most underdiagnosed cause of chronic daily headache and is entirely iatrogenic. The solution is reducing medication use, not escalating it.
